verdict.rationale: The lexical pattern affirms the core claim across both testaments. In 2Tim.3.16-17 the predicate of completeness rests on two cognate words from the same root, ἄρτιος (G0739, fitted, complete) and the perfect passive participle ἐξηρτισμένος from ἐξαρτίζω (G1822, finished out, fully outfitted), declaring the man of God complete and equipped πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν. 2Pet.1.3 parallels this with the perfect participle δεδωρημένης (G1433) governing πάντα τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν, a completed and enduring bestowal. The OT pole is the add and subtract merism: the Hiphil יסף (H3254, add) and Qal גרע (H1639, subtract) flanked by emphatic לֹא in Deut.4.2, repeated verbatim with the same אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה formula in Deut.13.1 (English 12.32), the add half alone in Prov.30.6, and rendered in Greek by ἐπιτίθημι (G2007) and ἀφαιρέω (G0851) in Rev.22.18-19, a real high vote cross reference chain in the store. Two honest limits keep this from being airtight at the word level. First, the strongest sufficiency words are rare: ἄρτιος and θεόπνευστος are each hapax, ἐξαρτίζω occurs only twice, so their force rests on cognate morphology and context rather than canon wide distribution. Second, the same add and subtract idiom takes a different object in Eccl.3.14 (God's deeds) and Num.36.3-4 (land inheritance), so the words forbid editing God's verbal revelation but do not by themselves fix the extent of the canon or the precise scope of every good work. The core proposition (Scripture renders the believer complete for faith and practice and forbids supplement) holds across law, wisdom, epistle, and apocalypse and is undisturbed by the variant forms on the cited verses.

scripture.force: πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος. The sentence predicates ὠφέλιμος (profitable) on every Scripture, then enumerates four functional uses with πρὸς plus accusative: πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, πρὸς ἐλεγμόν, πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ. The qualifier πᾶσα distributes the predicate across the corpus named by γραφή (G1124, 51 canon occurrences, stable sense). The load bearing adjective θεόπνευστος (G2315) is a hapax legomenon, its sole canon occurrence, so its sense (God breathed) is fixed by morphology (θεός plus πνέω) rather than by canon wide distribution.

ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος. The ἵνα clause states the purpose of the γραφή claim. Two cognate words from one root carry the weight: ἄρτιος (G0739, complete, fitted) and the perfect passive participle ἐξηρτισμένος from ἐξαρτίζω (G1822, finished out, fully outfitted). The perfect aspect marks a settled, enduring state. ἄρτιος is a canon hapax and ἐξαρτίζω occurs only twice, the other being Act.21.5 where ἐξαρτίσαι τὰς ἡμέρας means to complete or finish the days, which confirms the completion sense here. The scope πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν is unlimited as to good works, but the vocabulary delimits the result to the man of God being complete and equipped, not to answering every conceivable question.

Ὡς πάντα ἡμῖν τῆς θείας δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν δεδωρημένης διὰ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ καλέσαντος ἡμᾶς. The perfect middle participle δεδωρημένης (from δωρέομαι, G1433, 3 canon occurrences) governs πάντα τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν, the perfect aspect asserting a completed bestowal whose effect endures. The πάντα τὰ πρός plus accusative construction mirrors the πρός plus accusative of 2Tim.3.16-17 and is exhaustive over the domain of ζωή (life) and εὐσέβεια (godliness). The instrument is ἐπίγνωσις of the One who called. The clause does not name γραφή explicitly, so its bearing on Scripture specifically is inferential, but it asserts that the means of life and godliness has already been delivered in full.

לֹא תֹסִפוּ עַל הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה אֶתְכֶם וְלֹא תִגְרְעוּ מִמֶּנּוּ לִשְׁמֹר אֶת מִצְוֺת יְהוָה. The Hiphil יָסַף (H3254, add) and Qal גָּרַע (H1639, subtract) are each flanked by emphatic לֹא, and the deictic אָנֹכִי marks the speaker as Yahweh through the mediator. The infinitival purpose לִשְׁמֹר (in order to keep) frames the prohibition as a guard on the integrity of the commanded word (הַדָּבָר). ETCBC tags the clause as direct discourse with explicit negation, predicate, and complements. The store confirms יָסַף and גָּרַע co occur in the same verse only in Deut.4.2, Deut.13.1 (English 12.32), Eccl.3.14, and Num.36.3-4, so the pairing is a fixed idiom whose object here is the divine word.

אֵת כָּל הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה אֶתְכֶם אֹתוֹ תִשְׁמְרוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת לֹא תֹסֵף עָלָיו וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ. This verse (English numbering Deut.12.32) repeats the Deut.4.2 formula nearly verbatim. The store confirms its tokens include H0595 אָנֹכִי, H6680 צָוָה, H3254 יָסַף, and H1639 גָּרַע, the same add and subtract merism on the same object (the commanded word). It is an internal canon doublet that strengthens the closure prohibition rather than a separate witness, and it is the verse the cross reference apparatus points to from Deut.4.2.

אַל תּוֹסְףְּ עַל דְּבָרָיו פֶּן יוֹכִיחַ בְּךָ וְנִכְזָבְתָּ. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. The verb is again H3254 יָסַף (add) with the object דְּבָרָיו (his words, from H1697 דָּבָר). The store has this verse and confirms a high vote cross reference link to Deut.4.2 (38 votes) and Rev.22.18 (41 votes). Notably Prov.30.6 carries only the add half of the merism, no subtract verb, so it is the wisdom witness to the do not add prohibition specifically applied to God's words.

Μαρτυρῶ ἐγὼ παντὶ τῷ ἀκούοντι τοὺς λόγους τῆς προφητείας τοῦ βιβλίου τούτου. ἐάν τις ἐπιθῇ ἐπ' αὐτά, ἐπιθήσει ὁ θεὸς ἐπ' αὐτὸν τὰς πληγάς. The verbal play uses ἐπιτίθημι (G2007) twice: the human act of adding to the words triggers a divine act of adding plagues. This is the Greek rendering of the OT add prohibition, and the store confirms a strong cross reference back to Deut.4.2 (29 to 51 votes) and Prov.30.6 (41 votes), placing this verse in the same idiom chain. The bounded object is the prophetic βιβλίον (G0975) of this book.

καὶ ἐάν τις ἀφέλῃ ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων τοῦ βιβλίου τῆς προφητείας ταύτης, ἀφελεῖ ὁ θεὸς τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς. Mirror inverse of v.18: ἀφαιρέω (G0851) matches the Hebrew גָּרַע (subtract). The condition and consequence parallel completes the add or subtract merism bracketing the prophetic corpus. The threat is eschatological (the tree of life), which treats the integrity of the written word as bound up with salvation, but the words bound the prohibition to this book and do not by themselves define the limits of the wider canon.

כָּל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה הָאֱלֹהִים הוּא יִהְיֶה לְעוֹלָם עָלָיו אֵין לְהוֹסִיף וּמִמֶּנּוּ אֵין לִגְרֹעַ. Whatever God does endures forever, nothing can be added to it and nothing taken from it. This verse uses the SAME add and subtract pair (H3254 plus H1639) confirmed by the store, but its object is God's deeds (כָּל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה הָאֱלֹהִים), not a verbal corpus. It is the strongest internal evidence that the merism is a fixed Hebrew idiom of completeness whose object varies, which is why the vocabulary alone forbids editing God's revelation but does not by itself settle the extent of the written canon.

complicating_texts.resolution: Eccl.3.14 uses the identical add and subtract pair (H3254 plus H1639), verified in the store as one of only five verses where the two co occur, but applies it to God's deeds rather than to a verbal corpus. This shows the merism is a fixed idiom of completeness whose object shifts. It does not weaken the verdict where the object IS the divine word (Deut.4.2, Deut.13.1, Prov.30.6, Rev.22.18-19), but it does explain why the words alone forbid editing revelation without fixing the precise extent of the canon.

Num.36.3-4 also pairs H3254 and H1639, but the object is tribal land inheritance being added to or subtracted from one tribe to another. Confirmed in the store as a co occurrence of the same verbs. This is further evidence that the add and subtract pairing is a general idiom, not a technical canon formula, so the canon closure reading depends on the object being God's word, which is explicit only in Deut.4.2, Deut.13.1, Prov.30.6, and the Rev.22 echo.

Jesus promises the Spirit will guide εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν (into all the truth), which could be read as anticipating ongoing revelation. The syntactic context binds the promise to the apostolic hearers (ὑμῖν, second person plural), and the resulting apostolic writings are themselves the deliverable. The verb ὁδηγήσει (will guide) governs a completed body of truth, not an open ended stream, so it authorizes the apostolic completion now in Scripture rather than post apostolic addition.

προφητεία (G4394) appears as a spiritual gift here. The store confirms G4394 occurs 19 times, spanning both the communal Pauline gift (Rom.12.6, 1Cor.12-14, 1Th.5.20) and the bounded prophetic book (Rev.22.18-19). The Pauline gift is subject to discernment (1Cor.14.29 διακρινέτωσαν), whereas the Johannine usage names a closed βιβλίον. The single lemma carries two functions, so sufficiency for life and godliness lodges in the bounded written corpus, and the operation of the gift does not add binding doctrine to it.

παραδόσεις ἃς ἐδιδάχθητε εἴτε διὰ λόγου εἴτε δι' ἐπιστολῆς ἡμῶν names oral and written apostolic tradition as equally authoritative at the time of writing. The lexical point is that the antecedent oral apostolic content is now accessible only through the written record, so the παραδόσεις are not a surviving parallel channel but the same apostolic deposit now transmitted in Scripture.

ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τοῖς ἁγίοις πίστει. The adverb ἅπαξ (once for all) with the aorist passive participle παραδοθείσῃ marks an unrepeatable delivery of the faith. This construction foreclosing further deposits reinforces sufficiency by ruling out ongoing revelatory additions to the deposit.

variant_units_examined.note: The SBLGNT apparatus marks a verb form variation (ἐπιθῇ subjunctive against ἐπιθήσει future). Both preserve the prohibition of adding, so the semantic load on the verdict is unchanged.
Mood variation between ἀφέλῃ and ἀφελεῖ marked in the apparatus does not affect the merism of prohibited subtraction.
The marked variant between ἐλεγμόν and ἔλεγχον concerns the word for conviction or refutation. Both denote the same function, so the fourfold profitability scope is undisturbed.

variants.note: The bundle reports not_in_ecm_scope=true. Direct query of the lexical store confirms all 116 VariantUnit nodes are in 3John chapter 1, the only ingested ECM window, so none of the anchor verses (2Tim, 2Pet, Deut, Prov, Rev) carry ingested ECM data. The variant forms noted above are observable in the SBLGNT apparatus but do not bear on the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads ἄρτιος plus ἐξηρτισμένος and πάντα τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν as predicating that the written corpus already contains and supplies everything needed for the man of God to be complete for faith and practice. The perfect aspect on ἐξηρτισμένος and δεδωρημένης marks the equipping as a settled, enduring state, which forecloses a standing need for supplementary revelation. On this reading the add and subtract merism, where its object is God's word, seals the result.

Grants that the text predicates completeness but holds that the words leave the SCOPE open. πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν fixes the result as readiness for every good work, an ethical and ministerial scope, and ἄρτιος is a hapax, so the text does not by its own vocabulary specify whether sufficiency extends to every doctrinal or governing question beyond the equipping of the man of God. A reader holding this lens affirms the equipping claim but treats the breadth of sufficiency as not strictly delimited by these words.

Accepts that the add and subtract merism forbids editing God's verbal revelation, but observes from the store that the same H3254 plus H1639 pair takes a non verbal object in Eccl.3.14 (God's deeds) and Num.36.3-4 (land inheritance), and that Rev.22.18-19 bounds its prohibition to this book. On this lens the prohibition is decisive against tampering but does not on its own fix which writings constitute the closed corpus, a question the vocabulary underdetermines.

hermeneutics.notes: Grammatico-historical reading of πᾶσα γραφή as a distributive universal over the γραφή corpus, ἄρτιος plus ἐξηρτισμένος as redundant completion predicates (the second a perfect passive marking a settled state), and πάντα τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν as exhaustive over the soteric and ethical domain. The Deut.4.2, Deut.13.1, Prov.30.6, and Rev.22.18-19 chain applies the add and subtract merism to canonical boundaries, verified as real high vote cross references in the store. Progressive revelation is affirmed but terminates in the apostolic deposit (Jude.1.3 ἅπαξ). The competing lenses do not deny the equipping claim, they locate genuine underdetermination in the scope of every good work and in the extent of the canon, both of which the words leave open.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What is the relationship between Scripture and other potential sources (tradition, ongoing revelation, reason) in establishing what must be believed and practiced for salvation and godliness, and how far does the written corpus by itself reach?
stem_audit.notes: The stem 'Scripture is sufficient' states the conclusion at issue and presupposes that the question of sources is settled in Scripture's favor. The neutralized form opens the comparison of sources and adds the reach question. The verdict is still derived on the original stem because the anchor vocabulary does predicate completeness of the written corpus (ἄρτιος plus ἐξηρτισμένος, πάντα τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν δεδωρημένης) and forbids supplement (the add and subtract merism on God's word). The honest limit, surfaced in the competing lenses, is that the strongest sufficiency words are rare (ἄρτιος and θεόπνευστος are hapax, ἐξαρτίζω occurs twice) and that the merism idiom takes other objects elsewhere, so the words equip and forbid editing but underdetermine the precise scope and the canon's extent.

lay_summary: The claim is that Scripture supplies everything Christians must believe and how they must live before God, and that no fresh revelation is needed to be saved or to live godly. Reading the original languages, the case rests on a small set of unusually heavy words. In 2 Timothy 3 verses 16 and 17, Paul calls every passage of Scripture God breathed and profitable for teaching, conviction, correction, and training in righteousness, then states the goal with two words from one root, artios and exartismenos, which together mean complete, fitted, and fully equipped. The second is in the perfect tense, which marks a settled and lasting state, so the person who has the Scriptures is described as already finished off and outfitted for every good work. In 2 Peter 1 verse 3, Peter says divine power has gifted to us all the things that pertain to life and godliness, and the verb is again perfect tense, a completed gift whose effect endures. On the Old Testament side, Deuteronomy 4 verse 2 commands Israel not to add to and not to take away from the word God commands, using two Hebrew verbs, yasaph (add) and gara (subtract), as a pair that brackets the integrity of the commanded word. The same command repeats almost word for word in Deuteronomy 12 verse 32, the add half alone appears in Proverbs 30 verse 6 (do not add to his words), and Revelation 22 verses 18 and 19 close with the same pair in Greek, warning that editing the book brings matching judgment. Cross reference data in the database confirms these verses are genuinely linked with strong agreement. So where does divergence come from, on the words alone? Two places. First, the strongest sufficiency words are rare: artios and the word for God breathed each occur only once in the whole canon, and the equipping word occurs only twice, so their force rests on the shape of the words and their context, not on many examples to compare. Second, the very same add and subtract pair is used elsewhere for God's deeds (Ecclesiastes 3 verse 14) and for tribal land (Numbers 36), which shows it is a general idiom of completeness rather than a technical canon rule. That is why honest readers agree the text declares the believer fully equipped and forbids tampering with God's word, yet can still differ over the exact scope of every good work and over which writings make up the closed corpus, because the words equip and protect but do not, by themselves, draw those last lines.
